messages:
sam: Heads-up — escalated customer (AcmePayments) reporting a sudden spike in 403s and 504s. They say requests are being routed to a Europe region from their US on-prem environment. Suspect egress/NAT is changing source IP so our georouter picks eu-west-1. Logs attached in case thread needs them. :eyes:
alejandra: Got it. Any repro steps from the customer? Is it always for the same service endpoint?
sam: Customer provided a repro. Quick summary:
- Their requests to api.redwood.example/v1/generate return 403 token_mismatch or intermittent 504s
- curl -v shows server reporting client IP that geolocates to NL (eu provider) even though customer is in us-east datacenter
- They also see increased tail latency (~800-1200ms) starting ~2026-03-09 02:00 UTC
lucy: Can you paste the curl / response headers they saw? Also did they confirm any infra changes around the time?
sam: Paste from customer (redacted):
```
$ curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>" https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate
> GET /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
> Host: api.redwood.example
> User-Agent: curl/7.79.1
< HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
< x-redwood-region: eu-west-1
< x-request-id: req_abc123
< content-type: application/json
{ "error": "token_mismatch", "message": "token issuer mismatch for region" }
```
Also they ran `curl -sS ifconfig.co` from their gateway and got 185.45.76.12 which geolocates to NL. They swear nothing changed but mentioned a peering migration earlier that morning.
mike: Peering migration ring a bell — could be route advertisements leaking, or NAT was moved to a proxy cluster in EU. If the source NAT IP belongs to the EU pool, our georouter will steer to EU by design.
ops-bot: [alert] 2026-03-09T02:03:05Z — automated failover: us-east-1 capacity degraded, automatic fallback routed 12% of traffic to eu-west-1 for load shedding.
alejandra: ops-bot confirms a partial fallback at that time. Sam, can you ask customer for:
1) traceroute/tracert to api.redwood.example
2) output of `ip -4 route show` and `iptables -t nat -L -n -v` from their egress gateway
3) whether they use an egress proxy (squid/bluecoat) or cloud NAT gateway with Elastic IPs
sam: Yep asked for those. Customer provided traceroute + ip route. Key bits:
- traceroute shows next hop to their colo egress -> 10.0.0.1 -> then 198.51.100.5 -> 185.45.76.12 -> ... -> api.redwood.example
- `ip -4 route` shows default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0
- iptables nat shows a SNAT rule rewriting src to 185.45.76.12 (comment: "egress-proxy-v2")
lucy: Bingo. That SNAT address is in our EU IP pool (we onboarded partner peers last quarter). If the customer's egress SNAT uses an IP from an EU provider, our edge routing will treat it as EU-origin traffic.
mike: Two likely causes: 1) Customer's proxy pulled a public IP from a pooled EIP set that lives in EU due to peering migration, or 2) a transparent forward proxy in their colo forwards via an EU hop after peering change. Either way source IP changed.
alejandra: Short-term mitigation options for customer:
- Reassign egress gateway EIP from a US-range IP (if they control it)
- Configure proxy to preserve original client IP via PROXY protocol / X-Forwarded-For and ask our routing team for an exception to prioritize X-Forwarded-For header (requires auth implications)
- Route their requests through our dedicated US endpoint if they have Dedicated contract (bypass georouting)
sam: Customer tried swapping to a different NAT and confirmed `ifconfig.co` shows 34.201.10.55 (US). After that our logs show x-redwood-region: us-east-1 and 200s resumed. They still want a root cause since the peering change was their change window.
ops-bot: [note] runbook link: https://internal.redwood/runbooks/egress-georoute
lucy: Action items:
- Support: confirm and note in ticket that SNAT caused georoute mismatch and document repro
- Networking: check our peering announcement logs — want to see if partner advertised a block that overlaps customer's EIP pool or if we announced wrong prefix to partner
- Product: evaluate option to prefer authenticated token's home-region claim over source IP for region selection (security implications)
mike: For networking we should also audit any transparent proxies in partner path doing hairpin routing. A common mistake: proxy with dynamic public IP assignment gets an EIP from partner's EU pool.
alejandra: I created a support ticket update to the customer explaining: root cause SNAT -> EU IP, mitigation: reassign EIP to US or use dedicated us endpoint, and scheduling a sync with their infra team. I asked them to send VPN/peering config.
sam: Customer responded: they had a BGP change when shifting traffic to a new colo provider. The colo assigned a public IP block to their new NAT which was actually part of the colo's EU-facing pool because the colo's backbone is dual-homed and their apportionment logic gave them EU-range. They will request a US-range reallocation.
lucy: Good. Two follow-ups from our side:
1) Networking to validate that our georouting logic is strictly based on source IP and document edge decisions (to avoid surprises)
2) Product to discuss safe override for region preference when auth tokens claim a specific region (needs auth gating + anti-abuse checks)
mike: I'll open a networking ticket referencing this thread and include the traceroute + SNAT ip. Also adding suggestion: short-term we can accept X-Forwarded-For if request is TLS-terminated by our dedicated peering (we'd need to ensure mTLS / mutual auth).
sam: Customer thanked us and will confirm once colo reallocates. Closing as actioned but leaving open until they confirm reassign. :thumbsup:
ops-bot: [resolved] Support ticket #INC-2026-412 marked awaiting-customer.
alejandra: Noted. Adding internal postmortem template items — marking as "egress SNAT -> mis-routed by georouter". Will follow up if similar hits crop up. :memo:
lucy: Great catch everyone. Quick reminder for on-call: when seeing region mismatch always check egress SNAT IP geolocation first — saves a lot of cycles. :100:
